clinicalPearls: Presents in early infancy with neuromuscular irritability — generalised seizures, tetany and muscle spasms.
Profound hypomagnesaemia is accompanied by secondary hypocalcaemia that is refractory to calcium and vitamin D given alone.
The hypocalcaemia reflects impaired parathyroid hormone secretion together with end-organ parathyroid hormone resistance induced by severe magnesium depletion.
Autosomal recessive loss of function in TRPM6, a magnesium-permeable channel expressed in the intestine and distal convoluted tubule.
Both calcium and magnesium normalise only once magnesium stores have been repleted.
The defect combines impaired intestinal magnesium absorption with renal magnesium wasting, so urinary magnesium is inappropriately high for the low serum level.
Lifelong magnesium supplementation is required, often limited by osmotic diarrhoea at higher oral intakes.
Early recognition and repletion prevent permanent neurological injury.
reference.pathophysiology: Hypomagnesaemia with secondary hypocalcaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in TRPM6, which encodes a member of the transient receptor potential melastatin family — a magnesium-permeable cation channel bearing an intrinsic kinase domain. TRPM6 mediates active transcellular magnesium transport across the apical membrane of enterocytes in the small intestine and of epithelial cells in the distal convoluted tubule. When the channel is defective, intestinal magnesium absorption fails and the kidney cannot conserve magnesium appropriately, producing severe systemic magnesium depletion. Because magnesium is required both for parathyroid hormone secretion and for normal peripheral responsiveness to the hormone, profound hypomagnesaemia causes a functional hypoparathyroidism with parathyroid hormone resistance, and the consequent secondary hypocalcaemia drives the infantile seizures and tetany that dominate the presentation. The calcium abnormality corrects only when magnesium is restored, which distinguishes the condition from primary disorders of calcium or parathyroid regulation.
additionalDifferentials: Familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis (CLDN16 or CLDN19).
Gitelman syndrome (SLC12A3) with associated hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Isolated dominant hypomagnesaemia (FXYD2) and CNNM2-related hypomagnesaemia.
EAST/SeSAME syndrome (KCNJ10) with epilepsy, ataxia and a salt-losing tubulopathy.
Isolated recessive hypomagnesaemia due to EGF mutations.
HNF1B-related disease with hypomagnesaemia, renal cysts and diabetes.
Primary hypoparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency as alternative causes of infantile hypocalcaemia.
additionalInvestigations: Serum magnesium and serum calcium, interpreted together.
Parathyroid hormone level, characteristically inappropriately low-normal for the hypocalcaemia.
Fractional excretion of magnesium and urinary calcium to demonstrate the renal leak.
Electrocardiogram to assess for a prolonged QT interval.
TRPM6 genetic testing, with a wider hypomagnesaemia gene panel if negative.
Assessment for intestinal malabsorption as an acquired mimic.
Family studies given the autosomal recessive inheritance.
redFlags: Neonatal or infantile seizures unresponsive to standard anticonvulsants.
Hypocalcaemia that fails to correct with calcium and vitamin D.
Prolonged QT interval or cardiac arrhythmia.
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and lifelong magnesium supplementation the outlook is good and neurological development is preserved. Delayed treatment risks recurrent seizures and permanent neurological impairment.
pitfalls: Treating the hypocalcaemia with calcium and vitamin D while overlooking the underlying magnesium deficit.
Misdiagnosing the infant as having idiopathic epilepsy or primary hypoparathyroidism.
Stopping supplementation once calcium normalises rather than continuing magnesium for life.
Assuming the defect is purely intestinal and missing the coexisting renal magnesium wasting.
Not recognising the autosomal recessive pattern and the recurrence risk in siblings.
management: Replace magnesium as the definitive treatment, with lifelong oral magnesium salts titrated to the maximum tolerated dose and intravenous magnesium for acute crises
Recognise that calcium normalises only once magnesium is repleted, so do not rely on calcium and vitamin D alone
Manage acute tetany and seizures with intravenous magnesium alongside calcium, with airway and cardiac support
Limit the dose-limiting diarrhoea by dividing doses and using better-tolerated magnesium preparations
Monitor serum magnesium and calcium and the ECG for QT prolongation, adjusting supplementation accordingly
Refer to paediatric nephrology and metabolic services for co-ordinated long-term care
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive TRPM6 disorder and screen at-risk siblings
Escalate supplementation promptly during intercurrent illness or vomiting when magnesium losses rise and crises recur
